meta.title: A huge EU-India deal, Heated Rivalry, and a hefty $200k to Olympians

Our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news. On today’s episode: a HUGE trade deal between India and the European Union, all the hot hockey romance New Yorkers could ever want, and a heavy earnings purse for Olympic competitors, win or lose. Related episodes: Why the Olympics cost so much The surprising economics of digital lending For sponsor-free episodes of The Indicator from Planet Money, subscribe to Planet Money+ via Apple Podcasts or at plus.npr.org . Come see us live and hear stories from the upcoming Planet Money book and all about the making of it. Each stop has a special guest-- economists, business owners, other podcast friends. This will be a night of smart conversation and celebrating this book we're really proud of. And we've got a giveaway going. You can get a limited edition tote bag with your ticket purchase while supplies last. Details on that and how to get tickets in our show notes. Hope to see you in person soon. ANNOUNCER: NPR. [COIN SPINNING] [THEME MUSIC] WAILIN WONG: This is The Indicator from Planet Money. I'm Wailin Wong. WOODS: And I'm Darian Woods. And joining us from Planet Money is Kenny Malone. KENNY MALONE: I love being here for Indicators of the Week! WONG: Indicators of the Week! WOODS: Indicators of the Week! MALONE: One day, we'll get it all at the same time, one day. WOODS: So on today's show, we have a seismic trade deal between India and the European Union. WONG: We have all the hot hockey romance a New Yorker could ever want. MALONE: And listen, Olympians, I hope you're doing plenty of squats, because you're going to be lifting a heavy bag for participating in this year's games and future games. WOODS: Very intriguing. WONG: That's coming up after the break. MALONE: Did I use bag right, everyone? Can you help me? I'm not young and never have been. WONG: [LAUGHS] WONG: Indicators of the Week-- Darian Woods, you're up first. WOODS: So my Indicator of the Week is 25% of global GDP. And that's because the European Union just signed a trade deal with India that makes a trading bloc covering nearly one-quarter of the world's economic output. WONG: The world is busy banding together in the face of the US behaving kind of-- how do you say-- erratically? WOODS: Well, there are a couple of caveats here. First of all, this deal has been in development for about 20 years. So to tie it to President Trump is a bit of a stretch. MALONE: Uh-huh. WOODS: That said, an EU diplomat told the BBC that Trump's tariffs were a useful tailwind in the home stretch to get the deal agreed. MALONE: "Useful tailwind" is a euphemism I will be using for forever. That is excellent. WONG: I'm trying to think about these negotiators. How much turnover has there been? Is it the original team from 20 years ago? Or has it fully turned over? WOODS: It's probably a long invite list to the celebrations. But, you know, hold off on the tariff-free champagne, because the second caveat is that the deal still needs to be ratified. That means that India's cabinet, the European Union parliament, and EU member countries still need to approve it. So even if all that goes smoothly, it probably won't take effect until next year. MALONE: This is a multi-decade process. It's very old-school. I mean, hasn't Trump shown that deals can be made in weeks? 20 years? What is that? WOODS: Yeah, deals can be struck faster. That is certainly true. But you know, Trump has also shown how fast shotgun deals can unravel. WONG: Case in point, we had a deal with South Korea last year. And then a couple days ago, Trump threatened them with more tariffs. So it looks like not a great deal after all. WOODS: Yeah, he's claiming its legislature isn't living up to that deal. MALONE: So are we then to believe that the slower moving the trade deal is, like this one between the EU and India, that it perhaps will be more durable? Is that what you're insinuating here? WOODS: Yeah, I think so. So I'll give you an example, which is the automotive industry. India wants to protect its car companies, but the EU wants to sell cars to India. How does India let in more European cars into the country without hurting its politically vocal automotive industry? India agreed to lower its really high tariffs on vehicles down to 10%, but those low tariffs would only apply for 250,000 vehicles a year. So it's politically manageable for the Indian government. It's easing the door open and not just opening the floodgates and risking a backlash. MALONE: All right, so cross-borders negotiations done slowly. Wailin, you got any more cross-borders content for us? WONG: Oh. MALONE: I suspect you do. WONG: I do. I do. MALONE: I think you might. WONG: Yes, yes. My Indicator is 0 days. That is the wait time for checking out the e-book of Heated Rivalry if you're a New York Public Library cardholder. Heated Rivalry is part of a six-book romance series by Canadian author Rachel Reid. There's your cross-cultural content. These are queer hockey romances. Heated Rivalry is the basis of a TV series that first aired in Canada and then crossed over and became a huge hit on HBO Max here in the States. MALONE: I bet a lot of people are wanting to read this book after seeing the show. WONG: A prime example of someone who watched the series and then really wanted to read the book was Brian Bannon. He is the chief librarian at the New York Public Library. BRIAN BANNON: Yeah, I watched the series and was really taken with it. You know, I was a gay athlete in college. WONG: Hockey? Or what did you play? BANNON: I was a rower. Actually, I was also a swimmer. And so I watched the series, and then I immediately started wanting to read the books. I-- it was a number of months' [LAUGHS] wait time. WOODS: I mean, it's frustrating that there's even a holds list at all, because digital things can be copied unlimited for free. WONG: Yeah, so this is what's interesting about what the New York Public Library is doing. Libraries do not purchase e-books outright the way they buy physical media. They have to buy a license for an e-book. And the licenses come with terms. For example, maybe a title can only be lent out a certain number of times. Brian told me that with the Heated Rivalry license, the library pays each time someone checks it out. And right now, New York Library cardholders can check out any of the books in the series instantly through Valentine's Day. MALONE: Oh, wow. Cha-ching. WONG: So you can imagine this bill. Because Heated Rivalry has been checked out more than 5,000 times since they announced this promotion. And that's for Heated Rivalry alone. There's five other books in this series. Brian didn't have kind of the number with him when I-- when we talked for the final price tag, but I imagine it's pretty hefty. MALONE: What if this bankrupts the New York Public Library? WONG: [CHUCKLES] Brian assured me that they have, like, good budget planning, and that they think this is good. It's, like, good business for the library when they take advantage of these hot titles, because something like 2,000 people signed up for a library card over the weekend. That's, like, double what would happen in a normal weekend. So it's, like, they want to get people reading. They want to get people signed up for the library. So it's all good-- MALONE: I-- WONG: --I think. MALONE: I love it. I'd love to keep it in the sports world, in the money world, for one more Indicator, if you will. My Indicator is $200,000, and that is the amount of money US Olympians and Paralympians will now get if they compete, thanks to a private donor, win or lose. Win or lose. WONG: OK, and you're saying in addition to bonuses. Because they do get money when they win a medal, right? MALONE: Yes, yes. Famously, Olympic winners get all kinds of stuff from their home countries. Shout-out to The Wall Street Journal for a great recap on some of these. Poland gives its winners investment-grade diamonds. WONG: Ooh! MALONE: South Koreans get out of military service. When Indonesians won badminton gold, one got a house and cows, and both were promised a chain meatball restaurant. So-- WONG: A chain meatball restaurant? MALONE: I'm saying. But the US Olympic and Paralympic Committee not as interesting, perhaps more useful. They give athletes-- or have given athletes around $37,000 for gold and then less for the other medals. But this $200,000 that we're talking about, it is not that. This comes from a new $100 million donation from Ross Stevens, who founded a big financial services company-- big donor. WOODS: He must really love the Olympics. MALONE: He does love the Olympics, Darian. Do you not love-- how much have you donated for your Olympians in New Zealand? WOODS: I have not donated anything to my-- MALONE: All right, well-- WOODS: --Olympians. MALONE: --there you go. Listen-- WOODS: So good for him. MALONE: --I do think the most interesting thing about this is how this $200,000 is gonna pay out. So the Olympian or Paralympian is gonna get half the money-- so $100,000-- when they turn 45, or 20 years after the Olympic appearance-- WONG: Oh. MALONE: --whichever one comes later. And then the other $100,000 goes to their family or beneficiaries when the athlete dies. So-- WOODS: It's hard to use that money from beyond the grave. MALONE: Well-- WOODS: But I guess it's good for the family. WONG: So this is more of, like, a retirement or kind of, like, a inheritance for-- MALONE: 100%. WONG: --like, end-of-life-- MALONE: In fact-- WONG: --kind of thing? MALONE: I mean, exactly end-of-life kind of thing in-- for half of it. In fact, the funder, Ross Stevens, has said that this is about addressing financial insecurity for the athletes representing our country. And athletes would get this money each time they compete in the Olympics or Paralympics. And, you know, unlike many other countries, there is no government funding to reward our Olympic team. The US Olympic and Paralympic Committee relies on this kind of philanthropy plus corporate sponsorships plus selling broadcast rights to fund itself. And this $100 million donation is the largest donation they've ever received. So-- WONG: Wow. WOODS: Not a lifetime supply of meatballs, but it'll do. WONG: I'm surprised that the meatballs didn't come from the Swedish government. You said this was Indonesia. MALONE: I will say, I wasn't thinking about being good enough at something to be an Olympian, but you know, maybe I will now. Maybe I will. WONG: Well, now, you have a strong economic incentive to get-- MALONE: Yeah. WONG: --really good at a sport. MALONE: At cross-country skiing and shooting things from a distance. That's the biathlon, correct? Is that the one? WONG: That is the biathlon, yeah. MALONE: That's what-- that's what's gonna-- that's what's gonna to butter my bread, I think. Yeah. WONG: [LAUGHS] WOODS: Well, thank you, Kenny. I'm proud to have known you before your Olympic fame. But yeah, all the best. MALONE: [IMITATING SHOOTING] I don't know how to do a biathlon sign-off, but that seemed great. WONG: No, it was good Foley. I liked it. MALONE: [IMITATING SHOOTING] [MUSIC PLAYING] WONG: This episode was produced by Angel Carreras and engineered by Jimmy Keeley.
